strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaborative workflows influence interactive qualitative coding. Comparing workflows across tools is a worthwhile empirical contribution.

The evaluation includes three distinct methodological approaches and two contrasting corpora. Shared initial partitions within systems provide a useful control, and the dataset-dependent results offer informative exploratory observations.

The framework distinguishes consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness. The manual evaluation of 1,200 document-theme pairs, with two annotators and adjudication, provides evidence beyond embedding metrics; reporting Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.632 makes annotation reliability assessable.

The system descriptions, prompt templates, selected hyperparameters, and interview script provide useful methodological detail. Participant observations about control and theme refinement connect the evaluation to practical tool design.
weaknesses: The statistical analysis does not adequately establish the central significance claims. Section 4 describes only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous individuals per system, while Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying their observational units or effective sample sizes. Theme matches and document similarities share code-books and documents, and some participants are reused. Treating these observations as independent would inflate significance. The paper needs an analysis respecting this dependence, uncertainty at the coding-session level, and explicit handling of multiple comparisons.

The design does not isolate collaboration modality. Synchronous conditions use three-person teams, whereas asynchronous conditions evaluate individual code-books without consolidation. Team size and consensus therefore change together with synchrony, while time and effort are not reported. Reused participants always perform asynchronous coding first, introducing possible learning effects. The results support an exploratory comparison of these particular workflows, but stronger attribution to synchronous collaboration requires additional controls or narrower claims.

The automatic metrics are insufficiently validated as measures of qualitative code-book quality. Maximum-similarity matching permits multiple themes to match the same target, but theme counts, granularity, and matching sensitivity are not analyzed. Selecting documents nearest a centroid and then measuring embedding cohesion also mechanically favors cohesive subsets. These diagnostics do not independently establish deeper analysis or clearer themes; the description of uniformly substantial Climate improvements is particularly questionable when several differences in Table 2 are only 0.01.

The correctness evaluation has consequential reporting gaps. It covers only COVID, lacks uncertainty intervals, and labels Figure 4 as F1 without explaining how F1 follows from the document-theme judgments. The text states that asynchronous topic modeling is more accurate, but the plotted synchronous curve is higher through the first three cumulative quartiles and equal overall. Sampling weights and treatment of unassigned documents also need clarification, especially because Table 10 reports substantially varying LLM coverage.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied appendices. The stated total of 15 experiments is not clearly reconciled with evaluation across both datasets, and participant-to-session allocation is missing. The exact SBERT checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, and Climate-specific adaptations are unspecified. Code-books and analysis code are promised without an artifact link. The interview sample size and procedure for deriving the reported themes are also unclear.

Several general recommendations exceed the evidence. Two corpora differing simultaneously in domain, size, length, and repetitiveness cannot identify which characteristics explain collaboration differences. Likewise, one 3B LLM using explanation-generating prompts does not establish general limitations of LLM scalability. The useful exploratory contribution could support a revised submission, but reanalysis, reconciliation of reporting inconsistencies, and tighter claims are needed before a sound Findings recommendation.
